prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, which opened the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as my single preferred part and I have not changed configuration since round 1. After reading all eight statements and the chair's questions, the case rests on three things that none of the files dispute: a quantitative prediction (flat bands at a magic angle, 2011) that nature then confirmed, an experimental discovery (correlated insulating and superconducting states, 2018) reproduced by many independent laboratories, and a new experimental control parameter, the twist angle, that has carried over to other moire platforms. The citation I propose claims no pairing mechanism, which answers the chair's second question directly, and the credited trio splits cleanly into theory (MacDonald, Bistritzer) and experiment (Jarillo-Herrero) with unanimous agreement among the seven members who ranked it on who the names are. I do not rest this on the six-to-two split in preferences; I would hold the same position if the count were closer, because the science of the discovery is the part least in question. I record one correction to my own round-1 reasoning: I wrote that the 2016 and 2010 prizes were only neighbouring context, and I still think that is right, but I am working from memory of those citations, not from a checked source.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is timing and credit. The field is about eight years old, the superconducting mechanism is unresolved, and twist-angle disorder makes some device-level claims sample-specific, so a prize now honours a platform and a set of observed phases, not an explained mechanism. Credit is also truncated: Yuan Cao as first author of the 2018 papers, the earlier twisted-bilayer theory of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, and other moire groups are outside any three-name set, and my claim that the earlier theory did not predict the magic-angle flat band is recalled priority history that I have not verified in this exercise. I also see that B045 is the more mature and more cleanly attributed candidate, and that if the committee weights completeness over breadth, B045 is a defensible choice that I would not oppose. Where I differ from its supporters is on what carries more weight in the Nobel criteria: a prediction confirmed by experiment that opens a field, against a precision advance whose decisive practical event, the redefinition of the second, has not yet occurred.

responses.point: Kroll prefers optical lattice clocks (B045) for the cleanest two-name credit and a settled physics base, acknowledges that clocks may look like a third helping after the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and agrees that B038 has far more opening support.
responses.response: I accept Kroll's central point that B045 is settled physics with the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and I agree with him that the citation would have to say what is specific to lattices, namely the magic-wavelength trapping of a many-atom ensemble, and not simply stability and accuracy. That is the point where I would expect the committee to push back on the chair's earlier question of what new physics, as opposed to new accuracy, the clocks have revealed: I find the answer so far (tests of relativity and constants at the 1e-18 level, many-body effects in the lattice) real but still mostly a statement about measurement reach. I also take his disclosure of the stay in Hall's laboratory as a reason for him to say so openly if B045 reaches a vote, not as a reason to discount his scientific argument. I remain on B038 because a discovery that opened a new field weighs more with me than a measurement improvement, but I would support B045 if the committee decides otherwise.

responses.point: Lindroth answers the novelty objection by arguing that lattice clocks are a new measurement regime with new physics in it, such as many-body effects and relativity tests near 1e-18, and says the redefinition of the second is a likely consequence.
responses.response: Her answer is better than the objection as I put it in round 1: a regime in which gravitational redshift is resolved over millimetres and the clock itself becomes a many-body system is more than an engineering refinement, and I will not call it only an instrument. I still read the redefinition of the second as a future event that should not count as evidence of merit, and I read the unverified priority detail among lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley) as something the committee should check before a final vote. On her question about whether B038 is mature enough, I take it as a fair one and answer it this way: the discovery is mature in the sense that independent groups see the same phase diagram, while the interpretation is not, and the citation should be limited to the part that is. If the committee concludes that this distinction is not enough, then my position would move to B045 and not elsewhere.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B038 and treats the pairing mechanism as open but the discovery as firm, with the twist angle as a single tunable parameter, and in round 1 noted that the credited set will be contested because of Cao and the earlier theory.
responses.response: I agree with Mehlig that the discovery is firm even if the mechanism is not, and I would answer the chair's question about a conventional pairing mechanism the way I read his statement: it would change the interpretation but not the prediction-plus-observation structure of the citation, so my support would not change. Where I would be more cautious than his statement is on the weight of the single-tunable-parameter argument. It is a strong reason the field grew, but it is not by itself a reason for a Nobel Prize, and I do not want the committee to treat conceptual convenience as scientific merit. I also did not hear from him an answer to my round-1 question about a two-part prize pairing a topological-insulator part with B038, and with the three-person cap I continue to think it cannot be done without removing one of the B038 names.

responses.point: Olsson says the argument she takes most seriously is that B038 may be slightly early because the field needs a few more years to separate robust physics from sample-dependent behaviour, and she asks what new physics, not only new accuracy, the lattice clocks have revealed.
responses.response: I take the same argument seriously and I think her materials point sharpens it: robustness across laboratories is what makes the 2018 observation a discovery, but device-level reproducibility of fractional states and of superconducting domes remains partial, so the citation must stay at the level of correlated insulating and superconducting states and not claim a particular phase diagram. I do not agree that this makes waiting the better course, because the prediction-plus-observation structure is complete now and the committee has no assurance that a later year will be cleaner, only that the mechanism may be clearer. On her question about clocks, I put the same question to Lindroth above and I think her answer is a partial one. Her uncertainty about a second circuit-based prize so soon after 2025 is a reason I do not rank B026 among my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges an eight-year-old field with an open pairing mechanism as ready, or whether the age argument outweighs the discovery argument; this is the point on which I could still move to B045.

The priority history of twisted-bilayer theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto against Bistritzer and MacDonald) and the lattice-clock groups is recalled, not checked against a source, and I have not verified either account.
Whether the citation for B038 can credit the Jarillo-Herrero group experiment without leaving the first author, Yuan Cao, looking erased, given the three-name cap.
Whether B016 (IceCube) should be considered at all if I recuse, and how large-collaboration credit between Halzen and Karle would be handled; I do not rely on it in the preferred configuration.
statement.conflict_note: I am an astroparticle experimentalist on PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGO+ and XL-Calibur and I disclosed in round 1 that I would recuse from a final decision on B016 (IceCube), where I have no documented link to IceCube or its credited individuals. That disclosure stands and I do not rely on B016 in my preferred configuration, listing it only as an alternative that I would not vote on. I record no specific conflict for B038 or B045 from my profile, and I note that Kroll has disclosed a possible issue on B045 and Johansson on B026 and B007, which I take into account when weighing their statements.
